# Designing with SystemVerilog {#sec-sv-design .unnumbered}

## Goal for this week

- Tell the two styles of hardware description apart: behavioral and
  structural
- Describe sequential logic with `always_ff`: flip-flops, resets, registers
  with an enable, and counters
- Know what a latch is, and write code that cannot produce one by accident
- Describe combinational logic with `always_comb`: multiplexers and decoders
- Explain the difference between `=` and `<=`, and why each block uses one
  of them
- Assemble a design from smaller modules, and test it with a testbench

## Two styles of design

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
| | Behavioral | Structural |
|---|---|---|
| Describes | **what** a block does | **how** it is built from other blocks |
| Written with | `assign`, `always_*` | module **instances** |
| Example | a register, a multiplexer | a pipeline stage |

- Real designs mix both: leaf cells are behavioral, the levels above them are
  structural
- Start with behavioral
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
There are two ways to describe a piece of hardware in SystemVerilog, and a
real design uses both.

In **behavioral** design we describe *what* a block does: its outputs as a
function of its inputs and, for sequential logic, of its stored state. We
write that with `assign` and with `always` blocks, and leave it to the
synthesis tool to pick the gates and flip-flops. In **structural** design we
describe *how* a block is composed of other blocks: we create instances of
smaller modules and connect their ports with wires, much as one would wire
chips on a board.

| | Behavioral | Structural |
|---|---|---|
| Describes | **what** a block does | **how** it is built from other blocks |
| Written with | `assign`, `always_*` | module **instances** |
| Example | a register, a multiplexer | a pipeline stage |

The two styles meet at the leaf cells. In the HIPV SoC that we use as a
running example, the folder `rtl/generic` holds small, reusable cells
(`flopenr`, `mux2`, `mux3`, `adder`) written in behavioral style, and the
larger modules of the processor instantiate them structurally. This chapter
begins with the behavioral style, because those leaf cells have to be
written before they can be assembled, and ends with the structural style.
:::

## The `always` block

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
| Block | Describes | Runs when |
|---|---|---|
| `always_comb` | combinational logic | any signal it **reads** changes |
| `always_ff @(posedge clk)` | flip-flops | the clock edge |
| `always_latch` | latches | any input changes (rarely used) |

- Blocks run **concurrently**, not one after another
- Statements **inside** a block run in order
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The previous chapter described logic one line at a time with `assign`. That
is enough for an adder, but awkward the moment a function needs an `if` or a
`case`. For those we use an **`always` block**: a block of statements that
describes how a set of outputs depends on a set of inputs.

SystemVerilog has three kinds of `always` block for hardware, and which one
you use is dictated by what you are building:

| Block | Describes | Runs when |
|---|---|---|
| `always_comb` | combinational logic | any signal it **reads** changes |
| `always_ff @(posedge clk)` | flip-flops | the clock edge |
| `always_latch` | latches | any of its inputs changes |

The names are a promise to the tool: if the code inside does not describe
the kind of hardware the block name claims, the tool reports it. Older
Verilog has a single `always @(...)` for all three purposes, and a whole
class of bugs came from getting it wrong without any warning.

Two facts about `always` blocks are worth keeping in mind from the start.
First, every `always` block in a module is a separate piece of hardware that
exists all the time, like an `assign`, so they all run *concurrently* and the
order in which you write them does not matter. Second, the statements
*inside* one block run in the order written, like a small program. A block
is a description of hardware, not a function that gets called.
:::

## Sequential logic: describe the hardware you want

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
For every circuit in this chapter we follow the same four steps:

1. The **hardware** we want
2. Its **waveform**: what it should do over time
3. The **code** that describes it
4. A **walk through the waveform** to check the code
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Hardware description is not programming, and the habit that separates the
two is this: **decide on the hardware first, then write the code that
describes it.** If you cannot sketch the flip-flops and gates you expect,
you are not ready to write the `always` block, and the synthesis tool will
build something, but not necessarily what you meant.

So for every circuit in this chapter we follow the same four steps. First,
the hardware we want. Second, its **waveform**, which says what the circuit
must do over time and is the most precise specification there is. Third, the
code that describes it. Fourth, a walk through the waveform to check that the
code matches it. Learning to read waveforms is half of the work: it is also
how you will debug in simulation.

A convention for all the diagrams in this chapter: the clock rises at the
start of each numbered column, and input signals change in the *middle* of a
column, after the clock has fallen. That way an input never changes at the
same instant as a rising edge, and it is always clear which value the
circuit sampled.
:::

## The D flip-flop

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  q <= d;
end
```
:::

![A D flip-flop: `q` takes the value of `d` at each rising clock edge.](../images/waves/dff.svg){#fig-dff}

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The flip-flop is the memory element of synchronous design. It has a data
input `d`, a clock `clk` and an output `q`. At every rising edge of the clock
it copies `d` to `q`, and between edges it holds that value no matter what
`d` does (@fig-dff).

Follow the waveform from left to right. In column 0, `q` is unknown (the
hatched area): nothing has been stored yet. At the rising edge that starts
column 1, `d` is 0, so `q` becomes 0. In the middle of column 1, `d` rises,
and `q` does **not** react: the flip-flop is not looking. At the next rising
edge, starting column 2, it samples `d = 1` and `q` rises. The same happens
in reverse when `d` falls in the middle of column 3: `q` falls only at the
edge that starts column 4. A flip-flop is a circuit that looks at its input
at one instant per cycle.

The code is as short as the circuit:

```systemverilog
module dff (
    input  logic clk, d,
    output logic q
);
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    q <= d;
  end
endmodule
```

The sensitivity list `@(posedge clk)` names the event that makes the block
run, and the block runs *only* then. Between clock edges nothing happens and
`q` keeps its value: that holding is the memory. The operator is `<=`, the
non-blocking assignment, which we explain at the end of the chapter; for now,
remember that it goes with `always_ff`.
:::

## The latch

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
always_latch begin
  if (en) q <= d;
end
```

- Level-sensitive: transparent while `en` is high
- Almost always a **bug** in synchronous design
:::

![A latch: `q` follows `d` while `en` is high, and holds its value while `en` is low.](../images/waves/latch.svg){#fig-latch-wave}

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A **latch** is a memory element too, but it looks at its input for a whole
*level*, not at one instant. While the enable `en` is high, the latch is
*transparent*: `q` follows `d` continuously. When `en` falls, the latch
closes and `q` holds the last value (@fig-latch-wave).

In the waveform, `en` is high during columns 2 to 4. As soon as it rises,
`q` takes the value of `d`, which is 1. When `d` falls at the start of column
4, `q` falls with it, because the latch is still open. `en` falls at the start
of column 5, and from then on `q` stays 0: when `d` rises again in column 6,
the latch is closed and does not notice. Compare this with the flip-flop of
the previous waveform, where `q` could only change at a clock edge.

```systemverilog
always_latch begin
  if (en) q <= d;
end
```

A latch has no clock edge, so a signal passing through it can ripple along
for as long as `en` is high, which makes timing analysis difficult. In a
synchronous design we want flip-flops everywhere, and we use a latch only on
purpose. The reason to know it exists is that it is easy to build one
*by accident*, and the section on combinational logic below shows how.
:::

## Adding a reset

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
// Synchronous reset
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  if (reset) q <= 1'b0;
  else       q <= d;
end
```

```systemverilog
// Asynchronous reset
always_ff @(posedge clk or posedge reset) begin
  if (reset) q <= 1'b0;
  else       q <= d;
end
```
:::

![Synchronous reset: `q` clears at the next rising edge after `reset` rises.](../images/waves/dff_reset.svg){#fig-dff-reset}

![Asynchronous reset: `q` clears the moment `reset` rises, without waiting for a clock edge.](../images/waves/dff_areset.svg){#fig-dff-areset}

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A flip-flop that powers up with an unknown value is a bug waiting to happen,
so registers get a **reset** that forces a known value. There are two ways to
write it, and both clear `q` when `reset` is high. They differ in *when* the
clear takes effect.

With a **synchronous** reset (@fig-dff-reset), `reset` is just another input
that the flip-flop looks at on the clock edge. In the waveform `d` stays 1.
`q` becomes 1 at the edge that starts column 1. `reset` rises in the middle
of column 1 and `q` does not move; only at the edge starting column 2 does
the flip-flop see `reset` high and clear. It stays cleared through the edges
of columns 3 and 4 because `reset` is still high. `reset` falls in the
middle of column 4, and at the edge starting column 5 the flip-flop loads
`d` again.

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  if (reset) q <= 1'b0;
  else       q <= d;
end
```

With an **asynchronous** reset (@fig-dff-areset), the flip-flop reacts to
`reset` itself, whatever the clock is doing. The same stimulus now clears `q`
in the *middle* of column 1, the instant `reset` rises, not at the next
edge. It stays 0 while `reset` is high, and after `reset` falls it waits for
the next edge, at the start of column 5, to load `d`.

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk or posedge reset) begin
  if (reset) q <= 1'b0;
  else       q <= d;
end
```

This is why `reset` appears in the sensitivity list next to `posedge clk`:
the block must also run when `reset` rises. An asynchronous reset needs a
flip-flop with a dedicated reset pin, and its release matters: if `reset`
falls too close to a clock edge the flip-flop can misbehave, a problem we
return to when we discuss synchronizers. A synchronous reset needs a running
clock, but is just logic in front of the D input (or a dedicated set/reset
input on an FPGA flip-flop, like the one in the slice of the previous
chapter).

The HIPV SoC chooses one style for the whole design: its coding standard
requires a **synchronous** reset throughout. That is the style we use from
now on. Pick one style, use it everywhere, and know which one you picked.
:::

## Registers and the enable signal

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module flopenr #(parameter WIDTH = 8) (
  input  logic             clk, reset, en,
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] D,
  output logic [WIDTH-1:0] Q);

  always_ff @(posedge clk)
    if (reset) Q <= '0;
    else if (en) Q <= D;
endmodule
```

- From HIPV `rtl/generic/flopenr.sv`
- `WIDTH` bits wide, synchronous reset, **enable**
:::

![`flopenr`: after the reset, `Q` loads `D` only at the edges where `en` is high.](../images/waves/flopenr.svg){#fig-flopenr}

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A single flip-flop stores one bit. A **register** is a group of flip-flops
that load together, and in a processor most registers also need an **enable**:
a signal that says "load a new value at this edge", and otherwise "keep the
old one". A pipeline register that must hold its contents while the stage
ahead is busy is exactly that. This is the most-instantiated cell in HIPV:

```systemverilog
module flopenr #(parameter WIDTH = 8) (
  input  logic             clk, reset, en,
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] D,
  output logic [WIDTH-1:0] Q);

  always_ff @(posedge clk)
    if (reset) Q <= '0;
    else if (en) Q <= D;

endmodule
```

The module is the D flip-flop with a synchronous reset, plus one more
condition. `WIDTH` is a parameter, so the same description serves for a
1-bit flag and for the 32-bit program counter. The priority is spelled out by
the `if`/`else if` chain: reset wins, then enable, and if neither is active
there is no assignment at all, so the register keeps its value. That "no
assignment means hold" is legal inside `always_ff`, since a flip-flop
naturally remembers; it is the opposite of the rule for `always_comb`, where
it would build a latch.

@fig-flopenr shows the behavior. `reset` is high around the first edge, so
at the start of column 1 `Q` loads 0. `D` carries the values A, B, C, D,
changing mid-column. `en` is high for the edges starting columns 2, 3 and
4. At column 2 the register loads B. At column 3 `D` is still B, so `Q`
stays B. At column 4 `D` is C, so `Q` loads C. Then `en` falls in the
middle of column 4, and from the edge at column 5 on the register ignores
`D`, even though `D` keeps changing: `Q` holds C. @fig-flopenr-rtl is what
the synthesis tool builds: one flip-flop cell with clock, data, enable and
synchronous reset inputs, which is what an FPGA slice flip-flop provides
directly (the clock-enable and set/reset inputs of the previous chapter).

![The `flopenr` module (8-bit by default), drawn by Yosys from the real HIPV file. `$sdffe` is a flip-flop with **s**ynchronous reset and **e**nable.](../images/rtl/flopenr.svg){#fig-flopenr-rtl width=70%}
:::

## Counters: two ways to write one

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
// Way 1: one block
always_ff @(posedge clk)
  if (reset) count <= 4'b0000;
  else       count <= count + 1;
```

```systemverilog
// Way 2: next-state logic + register
always_comb
  count_next = count + 1;

always_ff @(posedge clk)
  if (reset) count <= 4'b0000;
  else       count <= count_next;
```

- Same hardware, different structure of the **description**
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A counter is a register whose next value is its own current value plus one.
Its waveform is the simplest of any sequential circuit: after the reset, the
output goes up by one at every clock edge (@fig-counter-wave). There are two
common ways to write it, and the best habit is to know both.

**Way 1: everything in one `always_ff`.** The straightforward form says, at
each edge, "if reset, clear; otherwise `count <= count + 1`":

```systemverilog
module counter4 (
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       reset,
    output logic [3:0] count
);
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) count <= 4'b0000;
    else       count <= count + 1;
  end
endmodule
```

![Timing of `counter4`: after the reset, `count` increases by one at every rising edge.](../images/waves/counter.svg){#fig-counter-wave}

At the edge starting column 1, `reset` is still high and `count` loads 0.
From then on `reset` is low, and at each edge `count` takes its own value
plus one: 1, 2, 3 and so on. When it reaches 15, the next `+ 1` wraps around
to 0, because the result is truncated to 4 bits.

**Way 2: next-state logic and a register.** The second form splits the
description in two. A combinational block computes what the next value
*would be*, `count_next`, and a plain register stores it:

```systemverilog
module counter4_next (
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       reset,
    output logic [3:0] count
);
  logic [3:0] count_next;

  always_comb begin
    count_next = count + 1;
  end

  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) count <= 4'b0000;
    else       count <= count_next;
  end
endmodule
```

![Timing of `counter4_next`: `count_next` is always one ahead of `count`, and the register copies it at each edge.](../images/waves/counter_next.svg){#fig-counter-next-wave}

The waveform now has one more signal (@fig-counter-next-wave). `count_next` is
combinational, so it changes as soon as `count` does, and is always one
higher. In column 1, `count` is 0 and `count_next` is already 1, but the
register ignores it at the edge starting column 1 because `reset` is high.
At the edge starting column 2 the register copies the 1, and so on.

Both modules synthesize to exactly the same hardware: an adder, a register
with a synchronous reset, and the feedback wire (@fig-counter-rtl).

![Both counter descriptions give this circuit, drawn by Yosys: the register output feeds the output port and the adder, and `reset` drives the synchronous reset input.](../images/rtl/counter4.svg){#fig-counter-rtl}

So why bother with the second form? Because it separates two questions:
*what is the next value?* (combinational logic) and *when do we store it?*
(the register). For a counter the answer to the first is trivial, and way 1 is
perfectly fine. For anything bigger, such as a state machine (see the
[next chapter](05b-fsm.qmd)) or a pipeline stage, the next-state logic can be
dozens of lines of `if` and `case`, and keeping it out of the clocked block
makes it far easier to read and to check. The HIPV SoC uses this idea in its
64-bit timer counter, `cntr`, which computes `plus_one = count + 1` with an
`assign` and feeds it to a register cell with an enable and a clear, instead
of writing the increment inside the clocked block.
:::

## Combinational logic

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- Output depends on the **current inputs only**: no clock, no memory
- `always_comb` re-evaluates whenever any signal it reads changes
- Blocking assignment, `=`
- Every output assigned on **every** path
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
We now do the same for combinational circuits. The method is identical:
hardware, waveform, code, walk through. The difference is in the waveform:
there is no clock, because a combinational output depends only on the
current inputs, so it changes as soon as an input does.

The block for it is `always_comb`. It re-evaluates whenever any signal it
reads changes. It is closer to a spreadsheet formula that recalculates on
every input edit than to a function you call. You write no sensitivity list,
since the tool works it out from the signals the block reads. The
assignment inside is the blocking `=`, which reads as "this is what the
output equals right now". There is no state to remember, which gives one
rule that matters more than any other: **every output must be assigned on
every path through the block**.
:::

## The multiplexer

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
// HIPV mux2.sv, with assign
assign Y = S ? D1 : D0;
```

```systemverilog
// the same, in always_comb
always_comb begin
  if (S) Y = D1;
  else   Y = D0;
end
```
:::

![A 2-to-1 multiplexer: `Y` follows `D0` while `S` is 0 and `D1` while `S` is 1, with no clock.](../images/waves/mux2.svg){#fig-mux2-wave}

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A multiplexer selects one of several inputs. The 2-to-1 version is the first
cell in `rtl/generic`, and HIPV writes it as a continuous assignment:

```systemverilog
module mux2 #(parameter WIDTH = 8) (
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] D0, D1,
  input  logic             S,
  output logic [WIDTH-1:0] Y);

  assign Y = S ? D1 : D0;

endmodule
```

@fig-mux2-wave shows what it does. There is no clock: `Y` equals `D0` while
`S` is 0 and `D1` while `S` is 1, and it changes the moment the selected input
or the select changes. At the start of column 2 `D0` rises, and since `S` is
0, so does `Y`. At the start of column 3 `S` rises, `Y` switches over to `D1`,
which is 0, and falls. At column 4 `D1` rises, `Y` follows. At column 6 `S`
falls and `Y` returns to `D0`, which is 1.

The same multiplexer in an `always_comb` block reads like this:

```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  if (S) Y = D1;
  else   Y = D0;
end
```

Both give the same circuit. The `assign` form is shorter for one line of
logic; the `always_comb` form is better when there are several outputs or
several conditions. For a multiplexer with more than two inputs, the
`case` statement is clearer than a chain of `?:` operators. HIPV's 3-to-1
multiplexer, written with a chain of conditional operators in the repository,
looks like this as an `always_comb` with `case`:

```systemverilog
module mux3 #(parameter WIDTH = 8) (
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] D0, D1, D2,
  input  logic [1:0]       S,
  output logic [WIDTH-1:0] Y);

  always_comb begin
    case (S)
      2'b01:   Y = D1;
      2'b10:   Y = D2;
      default: Y = D0;    // 2'b00, and 2'b11 falls back to D0
    endcase
  end
endmodule
```

The `case` compares `S` against each listed value and runs the matching
branch. The **`default`** branch is not optional: it makes sure `Y` is
assigned for *every* value of `S`, including the one the designer never
intended to use (`2'b11`), and values containing X or Z in simulation. The
synthesized circuit (@fig-mux3-rtl) is two comparators and two 2-to-1
multiplexers in series.

![The `mux3` cell as drawn by Yosys from the HIPV file: `S == 2'b10` selects `D2`, otherwise `S == 2'b01` selects `D1`, otherwise `D0`.](../images/rtl/mux3.svg){#fig-mux3-rtl width=75%}
:::

## The decoder

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  SlaveSel = '0;                                    // default
  if (Addr[31:16] == 16'h0000)  SlaveSel[0] = 1'b1; // IMEM
  if (Addr[31:16] == 16'h1000)  SlaveSel[1] = 1'b1; // DMEM
  if (Addr[31:12] == 20'h20000) SlaveSel[2] = 1'b1; // UART
  ...
end
assign DecErr = ~|SlaveSel;
```

- **Default first**, then override: no latch possible
:::

![An address decoder: one `SlaveSel` bit goes high for each mapped region, and `DecErr` goes high for an unmapped address.](../images/waves/decoder.svg){#fig-decoder-wave}

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A **decoder** turns an encoded value into a set of separate control signals,
and it is everywhere in a processor: the instruction decoder turns an opcode
into control signals, and the bus decoder turns an address into "which device
is being accessed". The second one is a clean example. The HIPV crossbar has
five slaves (instruction memory, data memory, UART, timer and GPIO), each
mapped to a region of the address space, and the decoder produces a
**one-hot** select, one bit per slave, plus an error flag for an address that
belongs to no slave. Here it is with the address map written out:

```systemverilog
module addr_decoder (
    input  logic [31:0] Addr,
    output logic [4:0]  SlaveSel,
    output logic        DecErr
);
  always_comb begin
    SlaveSel = '0;                                     // default: nothing selected
    if (Addr[31:16] == 16'h0000)  SlaveSel[0] = 1'b1;  // instruction memory, 64 KiB
    if (Addr[31:16] == 16'h1000)  SlaveSel[1] = 1'b1;  // data memory, 64 KiB
    if (Addr[31:12] == 20'h20000) SlaveSel[2] = 1'b1;  // UART, 4 KiB
    if (Addr[31:12] == 20'h20001) SlaveSel[3] = 1'b1;  // timer, 4 KiB
    if (Addr[31:12] == 20'h20002) SlaveSel[4] = 1'b1;  // GPIO, 4 KiB
  end

  assign DecErr = ~|SlaveSel;
endmodule
```

Read the waveform first (@fig-decoder-wave). Five addresses arrive one after
another, two columns each. The first, `0x0000_0040`, lies in the
instruction-memory region, so `SlaveSel[0]` goes high. The next addresses hit
data memory, the UART and the timer in turn, and each raises exactly one
select. The last, `0x3000_0000`, matches no region: every select stays low, so
`DecErr` rises. Only one select is ever high, because the regions do not
overlap.

Now the code. The first statement in the block is the important one:
`SlaveSel = '0` assigns the default, *every bit low*, before anything else.
Each `if` then overrides one bit. Because every bit of `SlaveSel` has a value
on every path, whatever the address, the block cannot build a latch, and none
of the `if`s needs an `else`. This **default first, then override** pattern
is the safest way to write `always_comb`, and you will see it throughout
HIPV. The last line uses the reduction operator from the previous chapter:
`~|SlaveSel` is true when no select bit is set.

(The real `obi_decoder` in the HIPV repository is the same block, with the
base addresses and sizes taken from a shared package, so that adding a slave
changes one file.)
:::

## Avoiding latches

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  if (sel) y = in1;     // no else: what is y when sel = 0?
end
```

- No assignment on some path: the output must **remember**
- Synthesis builds a **latch**
- Fix: a default value at the top, or an `else` / `default` branch
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The decoder showed the right way. Here is the wrong way:

```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  if (sel) y = in1;
end
```

When `sel` is 0, no branch assigns `y`. In a spreadsheet an unhandled case
would show a blank cell, but in hardware an output cannot go blank. If no
branch assigns it, the only way to keep it at *some* value is to remember the
previous one, so the tool builds a **latch**, the element from earlier in this
chapter (@fig-latch-rtl). It adds a storage element you did not intend, it
complicates timing analysis, and it is the most common bug in
`always_comb`. Tools warn about it, which is the reason to use `always_comb`
instead of the old `always @(*)`.

![What synthesis builds for an incomplete `if`: a latch whose enable is `sel`, so `y` holds its old value whenever `sel` is 0.](../images/rtl/latch_bug.svg){#fig-latch-rtl width=70%}

There are three ways to follow the rule. Give every output a **default** at
the top of the block, as the decoder does. Or write an `else` on every `if`.
Or give every `case` a `default` branch, as in `mux3`. Sequential blocks are
different: inside `always_ff`, a missing assignment simply means "keep the
value", which is what a flip-flop does anyway.
:::

## Blocking vs. non-blocking assignment

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
| | `=` blocking | `<=` non-blocking |
|---|---|---|
| Takes effect | immediately | at the end of the time step |
| Next statement sees | the **new** value | the **old** value |
| Use in | `always_comb` | `always_ff` |

- The rule has no exceptions
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
We have used two assignment operators in an `always` block, and the pairing
has been the same every time: `=` in `always_comb`, and `<=` in `always_ff`.
Now we can see why.

A **blocking** assignment, `=`, takes effect immediately: the next statement
in the block sees the new value. A **non-blocking** assignment, `<=`, only
*schedules* the update, which lands at the end of the current time step: the
next statement still sees the old value. The difference only shows when
there is *interdependency*, when a later statement reads something an
earlier one wrote.

### In combinational logic

Take three inputs and the function `s = c ^ (a ^ b)`, written with an
intermediate signal, once with each operator:

```systemverilog
module xor_gate (
  input  logic a, b, c,
  output logic s1, s2
);
  logic n1, n2;

  // case 1: blocking
  always_comb begin
    n1 = a ^ b;
    s1 = c ^ n1;
  end

  // case 2: non-blocking
  always_comb begin
    n2 <= a ^ b;
    s2 <= c ^ n2;
  end
endmodule
```

(Some tools refuse non-blocking assignments inside `always_comb`
altogether; the example is written this way only to show what would happen.)

![The two XOR descriptions: `s1` always matches `c ^ n1`, while `s2` is computed from the previous value of `n2`.](../images/waves/blocking_comb.svg){#fig-blocking-comb}

@fig-blocking-comb shows the result for the same inputs. In case 1, `n1`
updates immediately, and the next line uses the new `n1`, so `s1` is always
`c ^ n1`. In case 2, `n2` is only *scheduled* to change, so `s2 <= c ^ n2`
reads the **previous** `n2`. Compare the last two rows: `n` changes at the
start of columns 2 and 6, and at exactly those two points `s2` differs from
`s1`, because it still uses the old `n`. Case 1 models a combinational
circuit; case 2
does not, because its output depends on a stale value. Synthesis tools often
ignore the distinction in combinational blocks and build the right gates
anyway, which makes it worse: the simulation shows one behavior and the
hardware has another, a *simulation/synthesis mismatch*, the kind of bug that
is hardest to find.

### In sequential logic

The same experiment on two registers in a chain:

```systemverilog
module chain (
  input  logic clk, a,
  output logic f1, f2
);
  logic b1, b2;

  // case 1: blocking
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    b1 = a;
    f1 = b1;
  end

  // case 2: non-blocking
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    b2 <= a;
    f2 <= b2;
  end
endmodule
```

![Two registers in a chain: with blocking assignment `f1` follows `b1` in the same cycle, with non-blocking assignment `f2` lags by one more clock.](../images/waves/blocking_seq.svg){#fig-blocking-seq}

In @fig-blocking-seq the clock is drawn with two columns per period, so it
rises at the start of columns 1, 3, 5 and 7. The input `a` is high during
columns 2 and 3, so the edge at the start of column 3 is the one that sees it.
In case 1, `b1 = a` happens first, and `f1 = b1` then reads the *new* `b1`, so
`f1` gets the value of `a` in the same cycle: both change at the edge starting
column 3, and the second register adds nothing. In case 2, `b2 <= a` and
`f2 <= b2` are both evaluated before either update lands, so `f2` takes the
value `b2` had *before* this edge. `b2` rises at column 3, but `f2` only at
the next edge, at column 5, and it falls one edge after `b2` does, at column
7. That is a two-stage chain, which is what two registers in a row should be.
This is the behavior every pipeline relies on, and it is why the swap
`a <= b; b <= a;` works with `<=` and silently fails with `=`.

### The rule

| | Blocking `=` | Non-blocking `<=` |
|---|---|---|
| Update takes effect | immediately | at the end of the time step |
| The next statement reads | the new value | the old value |
| Use in | `always_comb` | `always_ff` |

`=` for combinational logic, `<=` for clocked logic, every time. Do not mix
the two in one block.
:::

## Structural design: module instances

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
flopenr #(32) pcreg (
    .clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(PCEnF),
    .D(PCNextF), .Q(PCF)
);
```

- *module name*, `#(parameters)`, *instance name*, *port connections*
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Behavioral modeling describes what a block *does*. **Structural** modeling
describes a block by how it is *composed* of simpler modules. Each copy of a
smaller module is an **instance**, and it has a unique name. Here is the
smallest useful example, a 4:1 multiplexer assembled from three copies of a
2:1 multiplexer:

```systemverilog
module mux2to1 (
    input  logic a, b, sel,
    output logic y
);
  assign y = sel ? b : a;
endmodule

module mux4to1_struct (
    input  logic [3:0] d,
    input  logic [1:0] sel,
    output logic       y
);
  logic y0, y1;                 // wires between the instances

  mux2to1 mux_low   (.a(d[0]), .b(d[1]), .sel(sel[0]), .y(y0));
  mux2to1 mux_high  (.a(d[2]), .b(d[3]), .sel(sel[0]), .y(y1));
  mux2to1 mux_final (.a(y0),   .b(y1),   .sel(sel[1]), .y(y));
endmodule
```

An instantiation has three parts. First comes the **module name**
(`mux2to1`), then the **instance name** you choose (`mux_final`), then in
parentheses the **port connections**. The notation `.a(y0)` reads "the
module's port `a` is connected to my signal `y0`". These connections by name
make the code easy to read and safe to reorder. There is also a positional
form, `mux2to1 mux_final (y0, y1, sel[1], y);`, which is shorter and fails
silently if someone later reorders the ports, so we avoid it. @fig-mux4-struct
shows the result: the tool leaves the three instances as boxes, exactly as the
hierarchy appears in the code.

![The structurally built `mux4to1_struct`: two instances select within a pair, and a third selects between the two results.](../images/rtl/mux4to1_struct.svg){#fig-mux4-struct width=80%}

### Parameters

A **parameter** makes a module configurable, which is how one description
serves every width. We have been using this all along: `flopenr` declares
`parameter WIDTH = 8`, and each instance picks its own. The override goes
between the module name and the instance name, after a `#`:

```systemverilog
flopenr #(32) pcreg (...);          // a 32-bit instance, by position
flopenr #(.WIDTH(32)) pcreg (...);  // the same, by name
```

The by-name form is safer when a module has several parameters. A
`localparam` is a constant inside a module that, unlike a `parameter`, cannot
be overridden from outside, which makes it the right choice for derived
constants.

### A real example: the program counter of HIPV

HIPV's fetch unit is almost entirely structural. Its program-counter loop is
built from three of the leaf cells we wrote above. The code is the actual
instantiation, reduced to this loop:

```systemverilog
module pc_unit (
    input  logic        clk, reset,
    input  logic        PCEnF,
    input  logic        PCSrcE,
    input  logic [31:0] PCTargetE,
    output logic [31:0] PCF
);
  logic [31:0] PCNextF, PCPlus4F;

  // next PC selection: sequential or redirect from Execute
  mux2 #(32) pcmux (
      .D0(PCPlus4F), .D1(PCTargetE), .S(PCSrcE), .Y(PCNextF));

  // PC register
  flopenr #(32) pcreg (
      .clk(clk), .reset(reset), .en(PCEnF), .D(PCNextF), .Q(PCF));

  // sequential PC
  adder #(32) pcadd4 (
      .A(PCF), .B(32'd4), .Y(PCPlus4F));
endmodule
```

Everything inside the parentheses is a wire name, and nothing here describes
any behavior: it only says which cell goes where. The register
holds the PC, the adder computes `PC + 4`, and the multiplexer chooses
between that and a branch target (@fig-pc-unit). Note how the signals form a
loop through the register, which is the only place where the loop is broken
by a clock.

![The PC loop of HIPV, drawn by Yosys with the three cells expanded into their hardware: the `$sdffe` register, the `+4` adder, and the next-PC multiplexer.](../images/rtl/pc_unit.svg){#fig-pc-unit}
:::

## Testbenches

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module tb_mux4to1;
  logic [3:0] d;
  logic [1:0] sel;
  logic       y;

  mux4to1_struct dut (.d(d), .sel(sel), .y(y));

  initial begin
    d = 4'b1010;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) begin
      sel = i[1:0];
      #10;
      if (y !== d[sel]) $error("sel=%b: y=%b", sel, y);
    end
    $finish;
  end
endmodule
```
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A **testbench** is a module that tests another module, the *device under
test* (DUT). It applies inputs to the DUT and, ideally, checks that the
outputs are right. Its inputs and the expected outputs are the *test
vectors*. A testbench has no ports of its own: it sits at the top of the
simulation, so everything it needs is declared inside as plain `logic`
signals and wired to the DUT by name, like any other instance.

```systemverilog
module tb_mux4to1;
  logic [3:0] d;
  logic [1:0] sel;
  logic       y;

  mux4to1_struct dut (.d(d), .sel(sel), .y(y));

  initial begin
    d = 4'b1010;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) begin
      sel = i[1:0];
      #10;
      $display("d=%b sel=%b y=%b", d, sel, y);
      if (y !== d[sel]) $error("sel=%b: expected %b, got %b", sel, d[sel], y);
    end
    $finish;
  end
endmodule
```

Everything happens in the `initial` block, which starts at time zero and
runs once. It holds `d` fixed and sweeps `sel` through all four values. After
each change it waits `#10` time units, `$display` prints the inputs and the
output, and the `if` checks `y` against the bit of `d` that `sel` selects.
The `#10` delay is not needed by the circuit, since a combinational output
settles almost instantly. It gives each test case its own slice of
simulation time, so the printed lines and the waveform stay readable. The
comparison uses `!==`, which also catches an `X` on the output where `!=`
would stay silent. `$finish` ends the simulation.

These statements (`initial`, `#10`, `$display`, `$finish`) exist only in
simulation. A synthesizer has no hardware for "wait 10 time units", which is
the line between the code you simulate and the code you synthesize.
:::

## Testbench for a sequential design

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```systemverilog
module tb_counter;
  logic       clk = 0;
  logic       reset = 1;
  logic [3:0] count;

  counter4 dut (.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .count(count));

  always #5 clk = ~clk;              // clock generator

  initial begin
    #12 reset = 0;
    #100;
    $display("count=%0d", count);
    $finish;
  end
endmodule
```

- The testbench must **supply the clock**
- `$finish` is essential: the clock never stops
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A registered design only changes on a clock edge, so the testbench has to
supply that clock; nothing else in the simulation will. Here it is for the
counter of this chapter:

```systemverilog
module tb_counter;
  logic       clk = 0;
  logic       reset = 1;
  logic [3:0] count;

  counter4 dut (.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .count(count));

  always #5 clk = ~clk;              // clock generator: period of 10 units

  initial begin
    #12 reset = 0;                   // release reset between clock edges
    #100;
    $display("count=%0d", count);
    $finish;
  end
endmodule
```

The separate `always #5 clk = ~clk;` has no sensitivity list and no guard,
so it keeps re-executing for the whole simulation and flips `clk` every 5
time units. That gives a free-running clock with a period of 10. It runs
concurrently with the `initial` block below it: every `initial` and
`always` block in a module starts at time zero and proceeds independently,
which is why the clock generator lives in its own block.

The stimulus holds `reset` high for the first clock edge (at time 5), then
releases it at time 12, between edges, so that no input changes exactly
when the clock rises, the same convention as in our waveforms. After the
remaining ten rising edges the counter holds 10, which `$display` prints. The
key difference from the combinational testbench is the waiting. A
combinational output is valid almost immediately after its inputs change, but
a register updates only once per clock edge, so a sequential testbench must
always budget enough simulated time, or wait for a specific number of
`@(posedge clk)` events, before checking the outputs.

`$finish` matters even more here. The clock generator never terminates on its
own, so without an explicit `$finish` the simulation would run forever.
:::

## Running a simulation

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
```bash
iverilog -g2012 -o sim_counter counter4.sv tb_counter.sv
vvp sim_counter
```

- Add `$dumpfile` / `$dumpvars` to write a waveform for GTKWave
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Any SystemVerilog simulator can run these testbenches. With the open-source
Icarus Verilog, you compile the design together with its testbench and run
the result:

```bash
iverilog -g2012 -o sim_counter counter4.sv tb_counter.sv
vvp sim_counter
```

The `-g2012` option selects the SystemVerilog language level. To look at
waveforms instead of printed lines, add two statements at the start of the
`initial` block, and open the resulting file in GTKWave:

```systemverilog
$dumpfile("tb_counter.vcd");
$dumpvars(0, tb_counter);
```

The waveforms you get are the same kind as the ones drawn in this chapter,
and reading them is the same skill. Checking results by eye does not scale
beyond a handful of signals, though. A testbench that compares outputs
against expected values, as ours does with `$error`, can be run again after
every change and report a clear pass or fail. Later in the course we move
this idea to a Python framework, cocotb, which makes writing such checks much
easier.
:::

## From design to the pipeline

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
- `always_ff` with `<=`: every register
- `always_comb` with `=`: every multiplexer, decoder, ALU
- Instances and parameters: how cells become stages, and stages a processor
- Next: these constructs, applied to a real five-stage pipeline
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Everything introduced here is the working vocabulary of the rest of the
course. `always_ff` with non-blocking assignment and a synchronous reset is
how every pipeline register is built, through `flopenr` and its siblings.
`always_comb` with a default at the top is how the ALU and the decoders avoid
latch inference. Instances and parameters are how those cells are assembled
into stages, and stages into a processor. The pipeline chapters introduce no
new syntax: they put these constructs to work on a larger example.
:::
